dom.name: Business & Management
tips: Job titles map differently from company to company (a Director may be a senior manager, a division head or a board member). Ask for business cards or an org chart before the assignment.
Numbers and acronyms (KPI, ROI, YoY) come thick and fast. Keep an acronym sheet handy and check whether the speaker says the full form or the abbreviation.
In negotiations, watch the register: keep the difference between 'there's some flexibility' and 'this is our bottom line', and don't turn a hedge into a flat statement.

tips: The competent authority is the Taiwan Intellectual Property Office (TIPO) under the Ministry of Economic Affairs, and the court is the Intellectual Property and Commercial Court. Patents fall into invention, utility model and design; utility models receive formality examination only, unlike the substantive examination of inventions, so keep them apart in negotiations.

A patent 'claim' has its own technical term (different in Taiwan and on the mainland) and is not an everyday 'assertion'. Statutes say 'infringement' in formal legal wording, while news and speech use a shorter colloquial form; choose to suit the occasion.

'License' means a contractual grant in agreements but a permit when issued by a government agency. The licensor grants and the licensee receives; confirm both terms with the other side before a contract meeting and then use them consistently.

dom.name: Transport & Rail
tips: Taiwan's High Speed Rail, Taiwan Railway and metro are three separate systems: THSR was built and is run by a private company, Taiwan Railway is now a state-owned corporation, and each metropolitan metro is run by a local government or its agency. Train types and routes follow their official English names (the Tze-Chiang is the Tze-Chiang Limited Express). Light rail and metro are different things by official name, so do not lump them together because they look alike.
'Platform' differs between Taiwan and the mainland. 'Fare' is the price of travel, while 'ticket' is the document you hold; keep the two apart.

tips: Taiwanese civil and architectural usage writes the word for 'slab' (bridge deck, floor slab) with a different character from the mainland. 'Structure' means a built structure in civil engineering but often 'construction method or detail' in architectural descriptions.

Contracts often feature design changes, extensions of time and liquidated damages for delay, which correspond to change order, extension of time and liquidated damages. Fix these renderings before a contract meeting.

Earthquakes, typhoons and floods drive Taiwanese design. 'Design earthquake' and 'return period' have fixed renderings, and a '100-year flood' means a flood with a return period of one hundred years, not one that happens once a century.

tips: An 'architect' in Taiwan is a licensed professional with a legal title; a 'designer' is a general term. Interior and industrial designers may not call themselves architects, so do not inflate their titles when interpreting.
A design 'brief' is the document in which the client states requirements, not a briefing in the sense of a presentation. 'Rendering' in architecture means a visualization image of the design.
'Sustainable design' in Taiwan often points to green building and the Green Building Label, while the American LEED is a separate rating system. The two can coexist but are not interchangeable.

dom.name: Religion & Philosophy
tips: Buddhism, Taoism and folk religion coexist in Taiwan, so keep them apart. 'Buddha' is rendered differently depending on context (the Buddha, Shakyamuni, a buddha in general), and 'Bodhisattva' always has one standard rendering.

Sanskrit and Pali terms have standard Chinese renderings (dharma, karma, nirvana and so on). If the speaker keeps them in the original, explain them first. 'Merit' in Buddhism means a religious term of virtue, not an ordinary 'advantage'.
In Taiwan, Christianity splits into Catholicism and Protestantism, with one umbrella term for both. Church, mass and service correspond to different Chinese words and must not be mixed.

dom.name: Gaming & Esports
tips: Taiwan's industry and the mainland use different everyday words for 'mobile game'. 'Game' splits into a word for arcade and console gaming and a general word for games; the Taipei Game Show uses the former in its official Chinese name.

tips: 'Textile' means woven or knitted goods in general, 'fabric' is the cloth itself (the mainland uses a different word), and 'garment' or 'apparel' means finished clothing. Brand and designer names are mostly kept in the original; only famous brands have fixed Chinese names (Chanel, for example). When unsure, say the original first and add the Chinese afterwards.

tips: Scientific terms must be exact: 'theory' in science is not an everyday guess, and 'significant' in statistics means statistically significant, not 'important'.

dom.name: Social Welfare & Human Rights
tips: 'Welfare', 'social security' and 'social insurance' are three different terms at different levels. 'Safety net' is commonly rendered as the 'social safety net'.

'Refugee', 'migrant' and 'new resident' are three different concepts. In Taiwan, 'new residents' mainly means foreign spouses and their children, which is neither migrant workers nor refugees.

dom.name: Psychology & Behavioral Science
tips: Split 'bias' by context. In cognition and decision-making Taiwan uses one word (roughly 'deviation-error'), prejudice against a group is a different word ('prejudice'), and a systematic statistical error is a third ('deviation'). Taiwan writes 'cognitive bias' with the first; mainland China usually uses the third.

'Effect', 'bias', 'fallacy', 'illusion' and 'heuristic' are different kinds of thing, so do not swap them when interpreting. Taiwan renders 'heuristic' with a word meaning 'shortcut thinking', while mainland China says 'inspiration-style method'; if the speaker mixes both, give both on first mention.

Many effects are named after people (Dunning-Kruger, Zeigarnik, Pygmalion, Weber-Fechner), and Taiwan and mainland China often transliterate the names differently. Media also use popular nicknames, for example short names for the Dunning-Kruger and IKEA effects. On first mention give the English name, and add a one-line explanation if the audience is unlikely to know the term.

Believing the past was better and things are getting worse.
Believing things have a fixed, defining essence.
Seeing objects only in their usual use.
An error in reasoning that undermines an argument.
Attacking the person instead of the argument.
rén shēn gōng jī (sù zhū rén shēn)
Distorting an opponent's argument, then attacking that.
Claiming one step will inevitably lead to disaster.
Presenting two options as if there were no others.
jiǎ liǎng nán (fēi hēi jí bái)
Treating two unlike things as equal.
Treating a claim as true because an authority said it.
Persuading with feeling instead of reasons.
Claiming something is true because many believe it.
Claiming something is good because it is natural.
Claiming something is better because it is new.
Claiming something is right because it has always been done.
Using the conclusion as its own proof.
Assuming the very point to be proved.

Assuming that because B followed A, A caused B.
A distraction that leads away from the real issue.
zhuǎn yí jiāo diǎn (hóng fēi yú)
Dodging criticism by pointing to the critic's own faults.
nǐ yě yī yàng miù wù
Answering criticism by raising a different wrong.
zhuǎn yí zhǐ zé (yǐ tā shì fǎn bó)

Redefining a group to exclude counterexamples.
méi yǒu zhēn zhèng de sū gé lán rén miù wù
Using one word in two different senses.
tōu huàn gài niàn (qí yì miù wù)
Assuming what's true of the parts is true of the whole.
Assuming what's true of the whole is true of each part.
Changing the criteria after they have been met.
Assuming a conclusion is false because its argument was flawed.
Picking data after the fact to fit a conclusion.
dé zhōu shén qiāng shǒu miù wù
Prefer the simplest explanation that fits the facts.
Items at the start are remembered best.
chū shǐ xiào yìng (shǒu yīn xiào yìng)
The most recent items are remembered best.
First and last items in a list are remembered best.
We judge an experience by its peak and its end.
Ignoring how long an experience lasted.
chí xù shí jiān hū shì
Unfinished tasks are remembered better (replication is shaky).
孤立效應（雷斯托夫效應）
The item that stands out is the one remembered.
gū lì xiào yìng (léi sī tuō fū xiào yìng)

chǔ lǐ céng cì xiào yìng
Pictures are remembered better than words.
tú xiàng yōu shì xiào yìng
Odd, unusual items are remembered better.
Memory differs for what is heard and what is seen.
Information tied to oneself is remembered better.
zì wǒ cān zhào xiào yìng
Failing to recall without the right cue.
xiàn suǒ yī lài yí wàng
Mood affects which memories come to mind.
xīn jìng yī zhì xìng jì yì piān wù

Google xiào yìng (shù wèi shī yì)
Later misleading information alters the memory.
cuò wù zī xùn xiào yìng
Remembering a fact but not where it came from.
Forgetting the source and mistaking it for one's own idea.
Taking suggested details as real memories.
A vivid, photo-like memory of a shocking event.
Remembering one's choices as better than they were.
xuǎn zé zhī chí piān wù
Negative feelings fade faster than positive ones.
qíng gǎn dàn huà piān wù
Bad events weigh more than good ones.
With age, people recall more of the positive.
Remembering the past as better than it was.
shí jiān yā suō xiào yìng

Forgetting what the person before you said.
